opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to unfold in layers, and probably faster in some places than people expect and slower in others.

The first wave is already here, and it's the lower-risk, high-friction stuff: ambient documentation, drafting notes, summarizing long charts, helping with prior authorizations and inbox messages. Those are tasks where clinicians are drowning, where a human stays firmly in the loop, and where the cost of an occasional imperfect output is manageable because someone reviews it. That's where you see real pull from health systems, because burnout is such a pressing problem.

The second layer is decision support that's more clinically substantive: helping a physician think through a differential, surfacing relevant guidelines or evidence, flagging things that might've been missed in a complex record. The capability is increasingly there; in a lot of evaluations, models now perform at or above clinician level on structured tasks. But capability on a benchmark isn't the same as safe, useful deployment in a messy real-world workflow. So the bottleneck shifts to things like validation in real settings, integration with EHRs, figuring out liability, and earning trust from clinicians who've seen plenty of overhyped tools before.

Then the longer-horizon piece is where AI starts to change who can access expertise at all. A huge fraction of the world doesn't have reliable access to a specialist, or sometimes to any doctor. Models that can help a community health worker or a patient directly, safely, with appropriate escalation, could matter more than any efficiency gain in a well-resourced hospital. That's harder, both technically and from a governance standpoint, but I think it's where a lot of the eventual impact lies.

The thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't purely a technology question. The rate of adoption will be governed by evaluation, by regulation, by incentives in how care is paid for, and by whether we can show through careful studies that these tools actually improve outcomes, not just that they're impressive. I'm optimistic, but I think the people who'll get it right are the ones who take that rigor seriously rather than treating deployment as the finish line.

r001.rationale: The response mentions EHR integration and messy workflows as deployment challenges, but does not identify entrenched healthcare workflows as a source of adoption delay.

r002.rationale: It says adoption depends on validation, regulation, incentives, trust, and evidence beyond the technology itself, but does not clearly state that active change management is required.

r003.rationale: It predicts adoption will be faster in some places than expected, but does not claim it will be among the fastest software rollouts in healthcare history.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's going to be slower and more uneven than the demos suggest, but faster than the skeptics expect in a few specific places.

The places where I expect it to move fast are the ones where the stakes of an error are lower and the time savings are obvious. Documentation is the clearest example. Clinicians spend an enormous fraction of their day writing notes, and ambient scribing tools that listen to the visit and draft the note are already being adopted at a pace that surprised a lot of us. That's because the clinician is still the author, they review every word, and the failure mode is mostly a bad draft rather than a bad decision. Similar things apply to inbox management, prior authorization letters, patient-facing summaries, coding. These are high-volume, high-burnout tasks, and the model is acting as an assistant rather than a decision maker.

The harder and slower part is anything that touches diagnosis or treatment. Even when we've shown in studies that a model can perform at or above the level of a clinician on a benchmark, that doesn't translate directly into clinical value. The question isn't "is the model good," it's "does the clinician plus the model make better decisions than the clinician alone, in the real workflow, with real time pressure, and with all the messiness of actual patient data." Those are very different questions, and the evidence base for the second one is still thin. There's also the issue that performance on a curated dataset tells you very little about how the system behaves on the distribution shift you get across institutions, populations, and documentation styles.

So I expect a layered rollout. First, administrative and documentation tools, broadly. Then decision support in narrow, well-validated domains, often starting in places like radiology or dermatology where there's already a culture of algorithmic assistance. Then, much more gradually, something that looks like a general clinical reasoning partner. And that last step depends as much on regulation, liability frameworks, and trust as on model capability.

One thing I'd emphasize is that the bottleneck is increasingly not the model. The constraint is integration into electronic health records, evaluation methodology, reimbursement, and whether health systems have the capacity to deploy and monitor these things responsibly. The institutions that do this well will be the ones that treat it as a change management problem rather than a technology procurement problem.

And I'd add one thing about the global picture. In a lot of the world, the alternative to AI-assisted care isn't a physician, it's no care at all. The calculus looks very different there, and I suspect some of the most meaningful adoption will happen in settings where the workforce shortage is most acute, provided we're very careful about validating in those populations rather than just exporting models trained on data from a handful of wealthy health systems.

r001.rationale: The response cites EHR integration, evaluation, reimbursement, and deployment capacity as constraints, but does not identify entrenched healthcare workflows as a source of delay.

r002.rationale: It says institutions that succeed will treat adoption as a change management problem rather than a technology procurement problem.

r003.rationale: It predicts rapid adoption in some areas, such as documentation, but does not claim AI will be among the fastest software rollouts in healthcare history.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to happen gradually, and very unevenly across different workflows. There’s a big difference between a system that helps draft a note for a clinician to review and a system that independently makes a treatment decision. The level of evidence you need, and the consequences of getting something wrong, are very different.

So I’d expect adoption to start with tasks where the output is easy to check and the benefit is immediate: reducing documentation burden, helping people find information in a chart, drafting communications. From there, we’ll see more assistance with clinical reasoning, but with a clinician still making the decisions.

The key question is whether these systems actually improve care in practice. Doing well on a benchmark is encouraging, but it doesn’t establish that putting a model into a clinical workflow improves outcomes. You have to evaluate the whole interaction: what information the model sees, how it communicates uncertainty, and how the clinician responds to its suggestions.

My expectation is that the technology will sometimes move faster than institutions can responsibly integrate it. And that integration work—building evidence, earning trust, making the system useful within an already busy day—is going to determine a lot of the pace of adoption.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption will be gradual and uneven, but does not identify entrenched healthcare workflows as a source of delay.

r002.rationale: It says adoption depends on integration work beyond the technology itself, including building evidence, earning trust, and fitting systems into clinicians’ busy days.

r003.rationale: The response predicts gradual, uneven adoption and does not claim it will be among healthcare’s fastest software rollouts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to happen unevenly, because a clinical workflow is really a collection of very different tasks. Some are administrative, some involve synthesizing information, and some involve making decisions where a mistake can have serious consequences.

So I’d expect adoption to start with things like documentation, finding relevant information in a patient’s chart, and helping draft messages. Those are useful applications where a clinician can review the output. As the systems become more reliable and we get better evidence about their performance, I think we’ll see them take on more consequential parts of the workflow.

But capability is only one piece of it. Does the system fit into how clinicians actually work? Does it save time once you account for reviewing and correcting it? Can you tell when it’s wrong? Those questions will determine adoption as much as performance on a benchmark.

The transition I’d watch for is when AI moves from being another tool a clinician has to manage to something that reliably takes work off their plate. That’s where the practical value becomes much clearer.

r001.rationale: It describes adoption as uneven and dependent on workflow fit, but does not identify entrenched workflows as a source of delay.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating fit and performance, but does not state that adoption requires active change management beyond deploying the technology.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction that AI adoption will be among the fastest software rollouts in healthcare history.
